1.note: Here and throughout the chapter, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

2.note: See how you translated this phrase in 1:52.

A **sign** is a kind of identifying mark or symbol. It is different from the “banner” referred to elsewhere in the chapter. The “banner” seems to represent each camp, while the **sign** identifies just one tribe or a portion of a tribe. If your readers would not be familiar with what a sign is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [with the symbol]
See how you translated **the house of their fathers** in 1:2.

Yahweh is using **from the front** as a common expression of his culture to mean “at a distance from.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [around but far away from the tent of meeting]

3.note: The implication is that these are the tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, as shown in verses 3–9. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And the three tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, who are camping]

It might seem that the expression **to the east to the sunrise** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [to the east]

This implies that this direction is in relation to the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the east of the tent of meeting]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the tribes that will camp to the east were actually **the banner of the camp of Judah**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be located near the banner of the camp of Judah]

Here, **the camp of Judah** represents the combined tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun who camp together under Judah’s leadership. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the camp of Judah, which includes Issachar and Zebulun]
This is the first of many times in this chapter that Yahweh uses the phrase **according to their armies**. See the chapter introduction for more information.

This is the first of many times in this chapter that Yahweh uses the phrase **the sons of** followed by a tribe name to refer to the men who belong to that tribe. See the chapter introduction for more information.
For these and the other names in this chapter, translate them as you did in chapter 1. See the chapter introduction for more information.

4.note: The phrase **his army and their counted ones** expresses a single idea. The phrase **their counted ones** tells more about **his army**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [as for his army, their counted ones] or [his army of counted ones]
The pronoun **their** refers to the army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the army’s counted ones]

The expression **counted ones** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Moses and Aaron with the help of the 12 leaders. Alternate translation: [and those of them whom you and the 12 leaders counted]
Translate this number according to the conventions of your own language and culture. See how you translated this number in 1:27.

5.note: The pronoun **him** refers to the tribe of Judah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [beside the tribe of Judah]

6.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

7.note: The implication is that the tribe of Zebulun would camp beside Judah, likely on the side opposite from Issachar. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The tribe of Zebulun will camp on the other side of the tribe of Judah]

8.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

9.note: See how you translated the same use of **counted ones** in 2:4.
See how you translated this phrase in 2:3. Alternate translation: [the camp of Judah, which includes Issachar and Zebulun,]

9.q: מְאַ֨ת אֶ֜לֶף וּ⁠שְׁמֹנִ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף וְ⁠שֵֽׁשֶׁת־אֲלָפִ֥ים וְ⁠אַרְבַּע־מֵא֖וֹת
9.note: See how you translated the large number in 1:46

The implication is that when the Israelites travel from one location to another, these tribes will begin moving first. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When traveling to a new location, the camp of Judah will start walking first]
If your language does not use ordinal numbers, you could use a cardinal number here or an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [before the other tribes]

10.note: See how you translated this word in 2:3.

Here Yahweh implies that these instructions refer to three tribes, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad, camping together under the **banner** of **Reuben**, as indicated in 2:10–16. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. See how you translated the similar expression in 2:3. Alternate translation: [The three tribes of Reuben, Simeon, and Gad will unite themselves under the banner of the camp of Reuben]

The implication is that these tribes will camp to the south of the tent of meeting. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the south of the tent of meeting]

11.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

12.q: וְ⁠הַ⁠חוֹנִ֥ם עָלָ֖י⁠ו מַטֵּ֣ה שִׁמְע֑וֹן וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י שִׁמְע֔וֹן שְׁלֻמִיאֵ֖ל בֶּן־צוּרִֽי־שַׁדָּֽי
12.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:5. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names.

13.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

14.q: וְ⁠מַטֵּ֖ה גָּ֑ד וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י גָ֔ד אֶלְיָסָ֖ף בֶּן־רְעוּאֵֽל
14.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:7. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names.

In 1:14, this man’s name is spelled “Deuel.” In Hebrew, the letters for “R” and “D” look very similar. So, it is likely that the name is misspelled here or in 1:14. However, it is not clear which spelling is correct. You could standardize the spelling, or you could include a footnote indicating that the name can be spelled either way.

15.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

16.q: כָּֽל־הַ⁠פְּקֻדִ֞ים לְ⁠מַחֲנֵ֣ה רְאוּבֵ֗ן מְאַ֨ת אֶ֜לֶף וְ⁠אֶחָ֨ד וַ⁠חֲמִשִּׁ֥ים אֶ֛לֶף וְ⁠אַרְבַּע־מֵא֥וֹת וַ⁠חֲמִשִּׁ֖ים לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וּ⁠שְׁנִיִּ֖ם יִסָּֽעוּ
16.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:9. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names and numbers. Note that this camp sets out “second.”

17.note: Here Yahweh refers to the Israelites changing locations along with **the tent of meeting** as if **the tent of meeting** were a person who **will set out with** them. See how you translated the same use of “sets out” in 1:51. Alternate translation: [And when the Israelites set out, the camp of the Levites will take the tent of meeting]

Here, **the camp of the Levites** represents “the people who descended from Levi.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with the people who descended from Levi]

This phrase means that **the tent of meeting** and **the camp of the Levites** will travel between the **camps** described in 2:3–16 and the **camps** described in 2:18–31. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [between one group of camps and the other group of camps]

Here, **they** and **their** refer to all the Israelite tribes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [As all the Israelites camp, so they will set out … according to the banners of their tribes]

The phrase **a man on his hand** was a common expression meaning each person in his own position. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each person in his or her own position]

18.q: דֶּ֣גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה אֶפְרַ֛יִם לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֖⁠ם יָ֑מָּ⁠ה וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י אֶפְרַ֔יִם אֱלִישָׁמָ֖ע בֶּן־עַמִּיהֽוּד
18.note: This verse is almost identical in structure with 2:10. The only difference is that this verse includes the direction (“to the west”) after “according to their armies.” Translate this verse in the same way you translated 2:10, changing only the names and the direction.

19.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

20.q: וְ⁠עָלָ֖י⁠ו מַטֵּ֣ה מְנַשֶּׁ֑ה וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה גַּמְלִיאֵ֖ל בֶּן־פְּדָהצֽוּר
20.note: This verse is almost identical in structure with 2:5. The only difference is that this verse does not include the phrase “the ones camping.” However, that phrase may be implied, and the UST models how to include it. Translate this verse in the same way you translated 2:5, changing only the names.

21.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

22.q: וּ⁠מַטֵּ֖ה בִּנְיָמִ֑ן וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֔ן אֲבִידָ֖ן בֶּן־גִּדְעֹנִֽי
22.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:7. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names.

23.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

24.q: כָּֽל־הַ⁠פְּקֻדִ֞ים לְ⁠מַחֲנֵ֣ה אֶפְרַ֗יִם מְאַ֥ת אֶ֛לֶף וּ⁠שְׁמֹֽנַת־אֲלָפִ֥ים וּ⁠מֵאָ֖ה לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וּ⁠שְׁלִשִׁ֖ים יִסָּֽעוּ
24.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:9. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names and numbers. Note that this camp sets out “third.”

25.q: דֶּ֣גֶל מַחֲנֵ֥ה דָ֛ן צָפֹ֖נָ⁠ה לְ⁠צִבְאֹתָ֑⁠ם וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י דָ֔ן אֲחִיעֶ֖זֶר בֶּן־עַמִּֽישַׁדָּֽי
25.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:10. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names and the direction.

26.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

27.q: וְ⁠הַ⁠חֹנִ֥ים עָלָ֖י⁠ו מַטֵּ֣ה אָשֵׁ֑ר וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י אָשֵׁ֔ר פַּגְעִיאֵ֖ל בֶּן־עָכְרָֽן
27.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:5. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names.

28.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

29.q: וּ⁠מַטֵּ֖ה נַפְתָּלִ֑י וְ⁠נָשִׂיא֙ לִ⁠בְנֵ֣י נַפְתָּלִ֔י אֲחִירַ֖ע בֶּן־עֵינָֽן
29.note: This verse is identical in structure with 2:7. Translate this verse in the same way, changing only the names.

30.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4.

31.q: כָּל־הַ⁠פְּקֻדִים֙ לְ⁠מַ֣חֲנֵה דָ֔ן מְאַ֣ת אֶ֗לֶף וְ⁠שִׁבְעָ֧ה וַ⁠חֲמִשִּׁ֛ים אֶ֖לֶף וְ⁠שֵׁ֣שׁ מֵא֑וֹת
31.note: This part of the verse is identical in structure with the first part of 2:9. Translate this part of the verse in the same way, changing only the names and numbers.

The implication is that when the Israelites travel from one location to another, the tribe of Dan will be the last group to start walking. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When traveling to a new location, the camp of Dan will start walking last]
If your language does not use ordinal numbers, you could use a cardinal number here or an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [after the other tribes]
See how you translated this phrase in 2:17.

32.note: See how you translated the same use of **counted ones** in 1:46.
See how you translated this phrase in 1:2.

32.q: שֵׁשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת אֶ֨לֶף֙ וּ⁠שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים וַ⁠חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת וַ⁠חֲמִשִּֽׁים
32.note: See how you translated this number in 1:46.

33.note: The author uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast between counting all the other tribes and not counting the Levites. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But they did not count the Levites]
The pronoun **they** refers to Moses and Aaron. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Moses and Aaron did not count]
See how you translated the same use of **in the midst of** in 1:47. Alternate translation: [together with]

34.q: וַֽ⁠יַּעֲשׂ֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כְּ֠⁠כֹל אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה אֶת־מֹשֶׁ֗ה
34.note: This sentence is a comment about what happened after the story as a result of the events within the story itself. This signals the end of a story. Use the natural form in your language for expressing the conclusion of a story. See how you expressed the similar idea in 1:54. Alternate translation: [And that is exactly what the sons of Israel did]
See how you translated this phrase in 2:17.

Here the masculine terms **man** and **his** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person according to his or her clans, in accordance with the house of his or her fathers]

The author is not referring to a specific **man**. He means each person in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each man according to his clan]
See how you translated the similar phrase in 1:2.
